entries.summary: A 25-metre concrete Christ on a rock spur above Les Houches, put up by a village priest on public subscription and inaugurated in 1934 as the dictatorships rose in Europe. It is across the valley from our route, not a detour off it: reach it on foot from Le Coupeau, either on the afternoon we arrive in Chamonix or before we start walking on day 1. Trying to reach it from the trail would mean dropping to the valley floor and climbing back.

eras.label: A priest and a mountaineering pope
eras.text: Claude-Marie Delassiat, parish priest of Les Houches, wanted a monument proclaiming the universal kingship of Christ — the theme of Pius XI's encyclical Quas Primas of 1925 — and he wanted it dedicated to that pope in particular. Pius XI had been Achille Ratti, a keen amateur alpinist who climbed Mont Blanc from the Italian side in 1890 and had stayed at Les Houches on his way. Delassiat launched a public subscription and spent about three years raising the money, backed by the bishop of Annecy, the Vatican and the people of the valley. The statue was intended to stand around forty metres tall; the subscription would not stretch that far, so it was cut to twenty-five.

eras.label: Building it without a road
eras.text: Georges Serraz, a Paris sculptor who specialised in religious work, won the commission by competition; Viggo Feveile, an architect based in the valley, oversaw the interior and a separate campanile for the Peace bell. There was no road to the site, so the workers laid rails and hauled everything up in tipper wagons and lived on the spot. The base was cast as concrete slices and assembled in place, while the head, arms and torso were modelled in clay, cast into plaster moulds and filled with concrete, with the last details worked straight into it while wet. The first stone was laid in August 1933, work stopped for the winter, and the finished statue — 500 tonnes on a plinth with walls 48 cm thick, to keep it standing in the wind — was inaugurated on 19 August 1934 and dedicated to peace. It is still the second tallest statue in France, after the Virgin at Mas-Rillier near Lyon, which Serraz also made.

eras.label: Listed
eras.text: The statue, its carillon and the surrounding parcels were inscribed on the French register of historic monuments, which means any restoration now has to be approved. An interior stair of eighty-four larch steps climbs to a platform hidden behind the halo; it is open by appointment only.

entries.summary: The saddle behind Les Houches has been a working crossing for two thousand years: a Roman legate set a provincial boundary stone on this ridge, Turner stopped here to draw, and in 1909 a rack railway arrived that was supposed to carry tourists to the summit of Mont Blanc.

eras.label: Where two Roman provinces met
eras.text: A gneiss pillar was cut and set up on this ridge on the authority of the emperor Vespasian, placed by his legate Cnaeus Pinarius Cornelius Clemens, commander of the army of Upper Germany. Its inscription says that Clemens “fixed the boundary between the Viennenses and the Ceutrones” — the Allobroges of Vienne on one side, the Ceutrones of the Tarentaise on the other. It was not only a line between two peoples: Vienne belonged to the province of Narbonensis, and the Ceutrones to the small alpine province of Alpes Graiae created by Augustus when Rome took the alpine passes. The stone was found in 1852 at Larioz, near the Col de la Forclaz-du-Prarion, and classified as a historic monument in 1875.

eras.label: Turner comes over on foot
eras.text: J.M.W. Turner walked from Chamonix towards Courmayeur in 1802, having carried a very large grey-washed sketchbook all the way from England for exactly this kind of country. He came through Les Houches and up through the woods to this col — the high point of his first day — and drew here before going on down the Val Montjoie, where he also sketched the bell tower of the church at Les Contamines. The sketchbook survives in the Turner Bequest at Tate Britain, and several of the Chamonix drawings became watercolours for his patron Walter Fawkes, shown at Fawkes's London house in 1819.

eras.label: The railway that was going to climb Mont Blanc
eras.text: In 1904 the Haute-Savoie council approved the engineer Henri Duportal's scheme for a rack railway from Le Fayet to the summit of Mont Blanc by way of the Aiguille du Goûter, entirely in the open air. Work began in 1906, and the first section reached this col — 1,653 m — where it was inaugurated on 25 July 1909 and opened to the public three days later. That year it carried an average of 103 people a day and took less than half what it cost to run. The line got as far as a temporary platform and refreshment stall at what was named the Nid d'Aigle, 2,372 m, on 1 August 1913, with the route beyond staked out towards Tête Rousse. The summer of 1914 began well and President Poincaré was expected in July; the war ended the project instead, and the post-war finances killed it for good in 1919. The tracks you cross here are the surviving part of it.

entries.caveat: Neither older claim is quite as tidy as it sounds. The boundary stone was found at the Col de la Forclaz-du-Prarion, further along the same ridge and not at this col, and it has not been there since the 1850s: the original stands under a shelter at Passy, with a facsimile beside the church at Les Plagnes since 1999. The Turner drawings are catalogued by the Tate without a location, and their identification as views from this col comes from recent research by Prue and John Bishop, who place them here because the tip of the Brévent only appears from this point. It is persuasive, but it is a re-attribution rather than the Tate's own title.

entries.summary: On 12 July 1892 a pocket of water inside the small Tête Rousse glacier, high on the slope you are looking at, burst and destroyed much of Saint-Gervais in half an hour. It remains the deadliest glacial flood recorded in the French Alps, and the reason the glacier is drained and monitored to this day.

eras.label: Thirty-three minutes to the valley floor
eras.text: Shortly after midnight on 12 July, about 200,000 cubic metres of water and shattered ice broke out of a cavern inside the Tête Rousse glacier at roughly 3,100 m. It stripped the ground bare going over the Rognes, gathering rock, soil, turf and fifty sheep, and became a debris flow — a lava of mud and gravel — as it swept along the right-hand moraine of the Bionnassay glacier below you and into the bed of the Bon Nant. By the time it reached the plain it had moved something like a million cubic metres of material and covered 77 hectares. It took roughly thirty-three minutes to travel the fourteen kilometres. In the gorge above Bionnay the flow stood twenty-nine metres deep; the hamlet was partly destroyed. Ten minutes after the burst it hit the thermal baths at Saint-Gervais, wrecking six of the eight buildings and killing at least 130 people there. The total dead and missing is usually given as at least 175. Bodies were carried down the Arve as far as Geneva.

eras.label: The man who went and looked
eras.text: Joseph Vallot, the Mont Blanc scientist who built and ran the observatory high on the mountain, investigated the empty cavity and left the measurements the story still rests on: a chamber roughly 20 by 38 metres, narrowing into a passage 3 by 5 metres that ran 85 metres to the foot of a 35-metre vertical shaft opening at the glacier surface. His contemporary account put the death toll above 200, which is why the figure quoted for this disaster still varies.

eras.label: It is still there
eras.text: Tête Rousse is small — about ten hectares — but water still collects inside it, and the valley below is far more heavily built up than it was in 1892. Since 2010 the glacier has been drilled, drained by pumping and kept under continuous monitoring, with evacuation plans for the villages beneath. The mountain you are photographing is under active surveillance for the same reason it made the news 130 years ago.

entries.summary: The church at the end of the day stands on the ruins of the castle that once guarded this valley, its bell tower built on one of the castle's towers. Getting it built took the villagers a ten-year lawsuit against the next parish down the valley, and money sent home by men who had left as pedlars.

eras.label: The castle of Montjoie
eras.text: A document of the Dauphine mentions the château de Montjoie for the first time, and calls the land around it Contamina, from the Latin condominium — the origin of the village's name. The castle watched the approach to the Col du Bonhomme and the frontier with the Tarentaise. When Savoy took the Faucigny in 1355 it lost its purpose, and it was gradually abandoned; by the census of 1561 there were three families living at La Contamine.

eras.label: Twelve hundred pages to get a parish
eras.text: Until 1760 the village belonged to the parish of Saint-Nicolas-de-Véroce, an hour's walk away over the hill. In 1751 the villagers petitioned the bishop of Annecy to be made a parish of their own. Their request ran to three pages; the lawsuit that followed, with Saint-Nicolas fighting to keep them, ran to twelve hundred and lasted ten years. The judgment authorising a church came on 24 July 1758. Saint-Nicolas appealed, which took another sixteen months, and was finally dismissed on 24 March 1760.

eras.label: A Piedmontese mason and the pedlars' money
eras.text: A contract was signed at Sallanches on 5 September 1758 with Domenico Gualino of Sastegno, a master mason from the Valsesia in Piedmont, to have the church finished by autumn 1760. The parishioners paid for it themselves with help from men born in the valley who had gone abroad as colporteurs — travelling pedlars — and made money in Germany, Austria and Hungary. Gualino died before the work was done and his son Joachim finished it. The first mass was said on 28 September 1760 and the bishop of Annecy consecrated the church to the Holy Trinity on 19 July 1766, an unusual dedication for this part of Europe. The tower was raised in 1776; the very slender spire came later, in the nineteenth century.

eras.label: Turner draws the tower
eras.text: Coming down the Val Montjoie on the walk that also took him over the Col de Voza, Turner sketched the church. His drawing shows the bell tower still under a plain four-sided pyramid roof, before the octagonal lantern, the flattened bulb and the needle spire were added on top — which is how you can tell the sequence.

entries.summary: A hermit is said to have settled at the head of this valley around nine hundred years ago to shelter travellers walking to the Col du Bonhomme and on into Italy. The baroque church that replaced his sanctuary was used as a stable during the Revolution, drew ten thousand pilgrims in a single day in 1873, and kept an art-historical riddle on its altarpiece until 1998.

eras.label: A hermit for the muleteers
eras.text: Tradition holds that a hermit — a Benedictine monk, by some accounts — settled here to take in and comfort the travellers passing through, and dedicated his sanctuary to Saint Antony, then the patron of muleteers and mountain guides. That choice tells you what the traffic was. A church has stood on the spot since at least the eleventh century, the small sanctuary grew into a parish, and by 1338 the village of la Gorge counted thirty households.

eras.label: The bishop walks up
eras.text: On 28 July 1606 François de Sales, then bishop of Geneva and later a saint, made the pilgrimage up this valley himself. At that time the inhabitants were few and too poor to support a priest of their own.

eras.label: The church you are standing in front of
eras.text: Claude Colliex, the new parish priest, set about replacing the building, and the work ran from 1699 to 1707. His architect was Jean La Vougna, who had just finished the church at Saint-Gervais and went on to build the one at Chamonix. Bishop Rossillon de Bernex blessed it on 25 August 1706. The façade carries its argument in Latin: over the door, EGO MATER PVLCHRAE DILECTIONIS — I am the mother of fair love — and on either side, “whoever finds Mary will find life” and, from Psalm 87, “her foundations are on the holy mountains,” which in this setting is not a metaphor. Fourteen oratories were built along the approach in 1728 as a rosary walk and turned into a way of the cross around 1840.

eras.label: A stable, and bells into cannon
eras.text: During the Revolution the church was profaned and used as a stable, and its bells were requisitioned to be melted down for artillery. It survived, and in 1804, after the population had collapsed, the parish was absorbed into Les Contamines.

eras.label: Ten thousand people in one day
eras.text: The nineteenth-century revival of Marian pilgrimage brought the place back to life. On 21 August 1873 a pilgrimage here gathered close to ten thousand people from across the region. The sacristy still keeps the banners made for that day by Flumet, Notre-Dame-de-Bellecombe, Saint-Nicolas-la-Chapelle, La Giettaz, Praz-sur-Arly, Megève, Combloux, Domancy, Servoz and Les Houches.

eras.label: The Trinity with four people in it
eras.text: The upper tier of the altarpiece, attributed to the Chambéry artist Jacques Clairant, originally showed the Coronation of the Virgin: Mary at prayer in the centre, flanked by Christ and God the Father. Somewhere between the late eighteenth century and the middle of the nineteenth it was taken apart — possibly to protect it during the Revolution — and when it went back up, God the Father was put in the middle. Art historians spent a long time calling the resulting four-figure Trinity a piece of theological daring. In 1998 someone noticed which way the cherubs beneath each statue were looking, and the original arrangement became obvious.

entries.summary: The steep paved ramp above the chapel is the real thing: a built pack road, cut and cobbled, that carried traffic from this valley over the Col du Bonhomme into Italy for centuries. What it is not, on any evidence anyone has produced, is Roman.

eras.label: The road to Italy
eras.text: This was a working route, not a path. From the head of the valley it climbed to the Col du Bonhomme, dropped to Les Chapieux and went on towards the Tarentaise and Italy, which is why a hermit set up a shelter at the bottom of it and dedicated his chapel to the patron of muleteers, and why a castle downstream at Montjoie was built to watch the approach. The paving you are walking on is what a maintained mule road looked like: cobbles set to shed water and take hooves on a gradient too steep for bare earth to survive.

eras.label: The Pont Romain
eras.text: Ten minutes above the chapel the path crosses the gorge on a stone arch known as the Pont Romain, a good place to look down at the tines — the potholes drilled into the rock by the torrent. The bridge is genuinely old and genuinely handsome. The guardian of the refuge just beyond it dates it to the 1780s.

entries.caveat: The name is the local tradition and nothing more. The tourist office and the commune both call this the voie romaine, but no excavation, inscription or document has been produced that dates any of it to the Roman period, and the bridge that shares the name appears to be eighteenth-century. Mountain pack roads across the Alps are routinely called Roman; where they have actually been investigated they usually turn out to be medieval or later, built or rebuilt for trade. Treat the paving as old and important, and the adjective as folklore.

entries.summary: The same family has fed travellers here for five generations. The licence was granted in 1842 to sell wine and food to the pedlars crossing the Col du Bonhomme, and the customers have changed from colporteurs to tourists to Tour du Mont-Blanc walkers without the business ever leaving the Mattels.

eras.label: A licence to sell wine to pedlars
eras.text: The chalet dates from around 1800. In 1842 the council of Les Contamines authorised Joseph Alexandre Mattel to run an inn in it, selling wine, food and whatever else the travellers needed — specifically the colporteurs, the travelling pedlars, who came up this valley and over the col. Men from these villages left as pedlars and some came back rich; the money that built the church down at Les Contamines came partly from them.

eras.label: Four rooms for people from the city
eras.text: It became a mountain hotel with four bedrooms, taking in townspeople who had begun coming to the mountains for their health and the view rather than to get to the other side.

eras.label: From hotel to refuge
eras.text: The Tour du Mont-Blanc arrived as a walking route in the 1970s and the hotel became a refuge, which is what it still is. Patricia Mollard, the guardian, is the fifth generation of the family to own it.

entries.summary: A stone cone about four metres high beside the path, which walkers have been adding to for generations. The custom of throwing a stone on it is real and still observed; the story about who is buried underneath is a legend, and a fairly recent one.

eras.label: Two English ladies
eras.text: The legend recorded by the commune says the mound covers the bodies of two English ladies found buried after a terrible storm on this exposed shoulder below the col. It is the kind of story the early tourist era produced in quantity, and it is not attested any earlier than the end of the nineteenth century.

eras.label: Throw a stone
eras.text: The place has a reputation for being unlucky, and the way to deal with that is to add a stone to the pile as you pass. Everyone who walks the Tour du Mont-Blanc contributes to it, which is why the cairn keeps growing — and why its present size says more about the number of walkers than about anything underneath.

entries.caveat: Nobody has established what, if anything, is buried here. The mound is mapped as an archaeological site and a tumulus, but no excavation report exists, and a cairn that everyone adds a stone to every summer is not a reliable object to date. The two Englishwomen should be treated as folklore, not as a grave.

entries.summary: For centuries this was the only straightforward way from the Val Montjoie into the Beaufortain, so almost everyone who needed to get between the two came over it: a medieval border, a thousand religious exiles walking home, a retreating army, the first naturalist to look closely at the rock, and an Italian division that never arrived.

eras.label: The col stops being a border
eras.text: Until the Treaty of Paris the col marked the edge of the Faucigny, held by the counts of Geneva. The treaty transferred the Faucigny to Savoy, and the crossing lost its frontier status overnight; the Val Montjoie below has belonged to the House of Savoy, and then to France, ever since. It became a border again in a smaller way after the 1860 annexation of Savoy, when the col formed one of the southern limits of the free-trade zone granted to northern Savoy — a status France cut back in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles.

eras.label: A thousand exiles walking home
eras.text: The Vaudois were Protestants from the high valleys of Piedmont, expelled by the Duke of Savoy in 1686. On the night of 16 August 1689 between nine hundred and a thousand of them crossed Lake Geneva by boat from Prangins, near Nyon, under the pastor Henri Arnaud and the veteran fighter Josué Janavel, and set out to walk back and retake their valleys. They came up the Bon Nant past Notre-Dame de la Gorge and climbed this col on 20 August at an average gradient of eighteen per cent, in rain, with snow to their knees. They crossed the Col de la Croix du Bonhomme, dropped down the Raja stream to Les Chapieux and slept at Séez. The column was not only soldiers: it carried pastors, students of theology, physicians and surgeons, a notary, a boatman, a butcher, an armourer and a wigmaker. They reached their valleys about fifteen days and 350 kilometres after leaving the lake.

eras.label: Saussure finds a rock that fits nowhere
eras.text: Horace-Bénédict de Saussure, the Geneva naturalist who put up the prize that led to the first ascent of Mont Blanc, came over this col and noticed sandstones and pebble conglomerates that resembled nothing else nearby. He gave them a paragraph headed “Grès remarquables” in the second volume of his Voyages dans les Alpes. Later geologists renamed them the Grès Singuliers — the singular sandstones — and they are still a puzzle: a 2020 study in the International Journal of Earth Sciences reads them as Jurassic river and delta sediment laid down while the crust was pulling apart, stranded in a landscape that is otherwise limestone. The pebbles underfoot near the Rocher du Bonhomme are rounded and sorted by size, and look as though they came off a beach this year.

eras.label: Four cannon left in the valley
eras.text: During the Revolutionary war in Savoy, a Sardinian force that had retaken much of the Faucigny was pushed back out by French troops through late September 1793. The Sardinians withdrew over this col, and four abandoned cannon were later found down at Notre-Dame de la Gorge — the guns had come this far up and no further.

eras.label: The path we are walking
eras.text: Napoleon III visited Savoy after its annexation to France, and the path over the col was rebuilt between 1861 and 1866 in the wake of that visit. A more ambitious plan followed and failed: the two ends of the old route nationale 202 — one stopping at Les Chapieux to the south, the other at Notre-Dame de la Gorge to the north — were meant to be joined over this col as part of the Route des Grandes Alpes. The road scheme was abandoned here, which is why the crossing is still a footpath.

eras.label: An objective never reached
eras.text: When Italy attacked France on 21 June 1940, the 2nd Alpine Division Tridentina, reinforced by the elite Duca degli Abruzzi battalion, was ordered to take the Col du Bonhomme and the Cormet de Roselend and push on to Beaufort. The Edolo, Tirano and Morbegno battalions came down off the Glacier des Glaciers from the Col de la Seigne towards Les Chapieux. They got no further than the head of the Chapieux valley, held up by French artillery and ski-scout sections and losing men steadily to frostbite in midsummer, and the offensive was called off on 24 June when the armistice was signed. No Italian soldier reached this col. The fighting itself is described at Les Chapieux, where it happened.

entries.caveat: Nobody knows where the name comes from. The rock above the col is the Rocher du Bonhomme and the pair is sometimes explained by a resemblance to a seated man, but no source establishes it. There is a well-documented etymology for a different Col du Bonhomme in the Vosges, and it does not transfer. Accounts of the Vaudois crossing also disagree: the col's own encyclopaedia entry dates the departure to 27 August and the march to 200 km in nine days, against the academic reconstruction followed here.

entries.summary: The col looks out over the pastures that make Beaufort cheese, and the whole crest around it was eventually given legal protection — not as wilderness, but to keep it being farmed. The engineered path down towards the Gittaz dates from 1892, and the damaged 1935 orientation table that once stood here is now kept on the refuge balcony.

eras.label: A path cut into the rock
eras.text: The descent from the col towards the Gittaz was engineered in 1892, cut as a walkway into the rock face rather than zig-zagged across the scree. It is a piece of nineteenth-century mountain path-building of the same ambition as the Crête des Gittes military path twenty years later, and it is oddly the one thing here left outside the protected area drawn around everything else.

eras.label: An orientation table in enamelled lava
eras.text: A table d'orientation was set at the col to name the summits of the two massifs it looks between, the Beaufortain and the Tarentaise. Like all of them from that period it was made of enamelled Volvic lava, a volcanic stone from the Auvergne that takes a fired glaze and survives being left outdoors at altitude for decades. This one did not survive intact; the damaged original is now kept under cover on the refuge balcony and a modern version stands in its place.

eras.label: The pastures put under protection
eras.text: The col and the ground on both sides of the Crête des Gittes were made a site classé — the French listing that protects a landscape from being altered — covering 576 hectares across the communes of Beaufort-sur-Doron and Bourg-Saint-Maurice. The orientation table had been listed separately a couple of years before, a protection repealed in 1944 once the larger one absorbed it. What the listing exists to keep is agricultural: the alpage grass between about 1,700 and 2,479 m, grazed by brown, black-eyed Tarine cattle, whose milk becomes Beaufort — a cooked, pressed cheese with its own protected designation of origin. The landscape you are looking at from the col is a working one, and is protected as such rather than as wilderness.

entries.summary: Built in 1922 as a luxury for its day — double rooms and a telephone at 2,443 m — then bombed to a ruin in the war and left for twenty-five years until volunteers rebuilt it by hand. The stone shell they saved is still inside the building you are looking at.

eras.label: A path dug to hide from the Italians
eras.text: The ridge running west from the col carries the Crête des Gittes, a path cut into the shale by battalions of chasseurs alpins in 1912. It was deliberately dug on the western flank of the crest so that troops moving along it could not be seen from the Italian side. It is one of the most spectacular stretches of trail in the Beaufortain, and it exists because this was a watched frontier.

eras.label: A telephone at 2,443 metres
eras.text: The Touring Club de France built the refuge from stone quarried on the spot, three storeys high in the manner of the period, which was to command the landscape rather than sit in it. For the time it was remarkably comfortable: double rooms, proper sanitation and a telephone. It ran until 1940.

eras.label: Shelled and abandoned
eras.text: The refuge was bombarded and partly destroyed in the fighting of the Second World War, in the same campaign that sent Italian battalions up the valley below towards this col. It was then left as a ruin for a quarter of a century.

eras.label: Rebuilt by volunteers
eras.text: Volunteers took on the restoration in 1965 and after three years' work the refuge reopened in the summer of 1968. The Club alpin français took over running it in 1983 and bought it in 1987.

eras.label: The new refuge around the old one
eras.text: An L-shaped extension and a terrace in wood and stone were built around the original stone building rather than replacing it, so the 1922 shell survives inside. The refuge now takes more than eight thousand overnight stays a year, and a full renovation is under way with reopening planned for 2029 — after which it should be staffed in winter as well.

entries.caveat: Sources disagree on the construction date by two years: the refuge's owners now give 1924, while the Touring Club de France announced the new refuge in its own journal in September 1922, which is the date followed here.

entries.summary: This hamlet was fought over twice in four years. In June 1940 a few hundred French alpine troops held the head of the valley against an Italian division; in August 1944 the Resistance made it their command post and beat off a German attack, losing ten men. One officer, Jean Bulle, appears in both stories.

eras.label: Barracks at the crossroads
eras.text: The valley of the Glaciers is the junction between the Beaufortain and the Tarentaise, and the Col de la Seigne at its head leads into Italy. When France created its alpine troops in 1888 the position was reinforced against a possible Italian invasion, and barracks were built at Séloge and here at Les Chapieux between 1890 and 1894.

eras.label: Fifty years of preparation, four days of use
eras.text: Two sections of the 80th fortress alpine battalion held the valley floor at the Séloge blockhouse and the Bellaval outpost, with ski-scout sections above them — Lieutenant Jean Bulle to the north of the col and Lieutenant Guidot to the south. On 21 June, under pressure from the Edolo battalion, both scout sections withdrew across the valley without losing a man, having done what they were there for: watch and slow. On 22 June, in atrocious weather, the Edolo pushed past the Mottets and took Bellaval, where Second Lieutenant de Castex was killed with his weapon in his hands. They could not attack the Séloge blockhouse: French artillery was too costly and they could not get their own guns forward to support an assault. The Duca degli Abruzzi battalion tried to go round the north and west along the walls of the Aiguille des Glaciers to take the Col d'Enclave, and failed under coordinated French artillery and Bulle's machine-gun fire — Bulle abseiled down the rock face to get an angle on the Italian infantry climbing towards him. Over 23 and 24 June the two Italian battalions lost heavily to French fire and to frostbite. The ceasefire on the morning of 25 June ended it.

eras.label: The combat des Chapieux
eras.text: Early in 1944 Lieutenant-Colonel Pierre Fourcaud and Captains Peter Ortiz and Thackthwaite were parachuted into the Tarentaise on Mission Union to arm and coordinate the local maquis; a drop at La Plagne in March armed the Tarentaise fighters and a large one at the Col des Saisies on 1 August equipped the Beaufortain maquis under Captain Jean Bulle — the same Bulle who had held the ridge above here in 1940. With the Germans in Bourg-Saint-Maurice, the Tarentaise maquis put its command post at Les Chapieux, ten kilometres north of the town, and Lieutenant Émile Paganon's section blocked the road from the south. On the night of 21–22 August the Germans came instead from the west, out of the combe de la Neuva, having crossed over by the Presset refuge and the Col du Grand Fond. Paganon's men were quickly outnumbered; reinforcements from the compagnie du Lac, a Beaufortain section, evened the fight, and the Germans were driven off — burning the buildings at Les Chapieux as they went. Ten of the maquisards were killed. Jean Bulle was murdered by the Germans that same day at Albertville, while negotiating the surrender of the garrison there; the battalion formed by merging these maquis was named after him and went on to help liberate the Tarentaise.

eras.label: The stele at the edge of the hamlet
eras.text: A memorial stone at the edge of Les Chapieux records the fighting, and there is a commemoration here every year attended by a detachment of the 7th battalion of chasseurs alpins. Descendants of the men involved still come; Jean Bulle's grandson and great-grandson attended the eightieth anniversary in 2024.

entries.summary: The frontier itself, and for most of its history a working one: a pass named in medieval charters, a smuggling route the Sardinian customs patrolled, the viewpoint an Alpine Club president singled out in 1863, and in June 1940 the line an Italian division crossed to attack a France that had already lost.

eras.label: A named crossing into the Aosta valley
eras.text: The col was in use in Roman times and stayed in use through the medieval centuries, when it acquired the name it still carries. Medieval documents give it as Mons Senae, Collium de Senia and Alpis Seniae. High passes like this one were open for several months a year in that period, and the Seigne was one of the doors into the Aosta valley for people and goods moving to and from France — which is why it was worth naming in a charter at all.

eras.label: Smugglers and the men paid to stop them
eras.text: The Seigne, like the Petit-Saint-Bernard and the Col du Mont, was for a long time a smugglers' road. What crossed it was tobacco and alcohol, salt, silk and lace, and on occasion livestock driven over the top. Against them were the gabelous, the customs men of the Sardinian salt monopoly, and a good number of smugglers were caught. There was once a building down at Les Mottets, where our day begins, that housed the customs officers posted to watch this side of the col.

eras.label: John Ball puts it in the guidebook
eras.text: The tour of Mont Blanc and this col in particular took hold in the accounts of English travellers and alpinists from 1863. John Ball, first president of the Alpine Club, named the Col de la Seigne among the finest viewpoints on the whole circuit, writing that it would always make this part of the road extremely interesting to any true lover of nature. The judgement has held: the reveal of the Italian face of Mont Blanc from the top is still the reason to be here early.

eras.label: The attack that came over the top
eras.text: Italy declared war on 11 June 1940 but did not move until the 21st. At the Seigne the advance met two sections of scout-skiers, one from the 80th fortress alpine battalion and one from the 7th battalion of chasseurs alpins, who fought a delaying action and pulled back across the valley on 22 June — to the Col du Bonhomme and the Col d'Enclave respectively. The Edolo battalion of the 5th Alpini came over the col in bad weather and under accurate French artillery, took the Bellaval work on 22 June where sous-lieutenant de Castex was killed resisting, and was stopped short of Séloge. Fortifications and firing positions from that summer are still recognisable on the ground around the col.

entries.caveat: The name has two competing explanations and no settled answer. The medieval forms point to the Latin signum, a signal, giving a col of the signal-fire. But the Celtic word sange means marshy ground, which describes the Combal flats further down rather than the col itself. Nobody has established which is right.

entries.summary: A small barracks built in the 1930s to watch the French border, used as a jumping-off point for the 1940 attack, then raided after the war for the skis the retreating Germans left behind — which is how the Mont Blanc ski school got started again. It is now a cross-border education centre and you can go in.

eras.label: An outpost on a nervous border
eras.text: The Casermetta — the little barracks — was built as a permanently garrisoned post on the Italian side of the frontier, at 2,365 m in the commune of Courmayeur. Through the 1930s, as relations between the two countries deteriorated, the Mont Blanc sector became a training ground for large and deliberately visible high-altitude military exercises. The building belongs to that decade of standing watch on a border nobody expected to stay quiet.

eras.label: The darkest thing it saw
eras.text: In June 1940 the Col de la Seigne was one of the axes of the Italian attack on a France already beaten by Germany, and the Casermetta sat directly behind it. This is the episode its own custodians describe as the darkest in the building's history. The remains of fortifications and gun positions from that summer are still visible in the ground around it.

eras.label: Skis taken off a retreating army
eras.text: In the winter of 1945 a group of trainee ski instructors under Francis Salluard set out to restart the Scuola di Sci Monte Bianco. They had almost no money and no equipment. What they did have was the white ash skis the German army had abandoned at the Col de la Seigne during its hurried retreat after 25 April, and they took them. The ski school was rebuilt on salvaged military kit.

eras.label: Rebuilt as somewhere to learn
eras.text: By the start of the 2000s the building was in poor condition. It was rebuilt as a visitor and environmental education centre with European money under the Interreg IIIA Alcotra France–Italy programme, and now runs entirely on renewable energy. It belongs to the Autonomous Region of Valle d'Aosta and is managed by the Fondazione Montagna Sicura, doubles as a station for the regional forestry corps and the Sentinelles des Alpes network, and is where the count of walkers passing on the Tour du Mont-Blanc is actually taken. Inside there is a relief model of the massif and a set of panels on what is around you.

entries.summary: A refuge an engineer built as a memorial to two women in his family who died in these mountains — his wife Elisabetta, whose name it carries, and his sister Teresa. He gave it to the Milan section of the Italian Alpine Club, which still owns it.

eras.label: Built for Elisabetta and Teresa
eras.text: The refuge was commissioned by the engineer Giuseppe Soldini in memory of his wife, Elisabetta Montanaro, after whom it is named, and of his sister, Teresa Grandi, who was killed in the mountains. It was inaugurated in 1953 and given to the Milan section of the Club Alpino Italiano, which owns it still. Its full name, rarely used, is the Rifugio Elisabetta Soldini Montanaro. It stands on the grass terrace of the Alpe Inférieure de la Lex Blanche, under the Pyramides Calcaires and in view of the Aiguille des Glaciers.

eras.label: Enlarged for the walkers
eras.text: The building was substantially rebuilt and extended, gaining modern services and a large winter room that stays open when the refuge is not staffed. The work turned a memorial hut into one of the working links in the chain of refuges that make the Italian side of the Tour du Mont-Blanc walkable in stages. It is also the final stage of the Alta Via della Valle d'Aosta number 2, and now sleeps around eighty.

entries.caveat: Where Elisabetta died is not firmly established. The Milan section's own page attaches the phrase killed in the mountains to Giuseppe's sister Teresa and does not say how Elisabetta died; a hiking gazetteer states that Elisabetta fell on the Mont de la Saxe, the ridge above Courmayeur that day 4 climbs. The memorial to both women is not in doubt, but that detail rests on the weaker source.

entries.summary: These flats are where alpine glaciology was partly worked out. De Saussure looked at the Miage in 1779, Forbes mapped the lake in 1843, and Italian geologists surveyed it every few decades after that — which is why there is a continuous record of this one lake going back over 160 years, and why we know the larger lake that once filled the valley here has gone.

eras.label: Saussure comes to look at the ice
eras.text: Horace-Bénédict de Saussure made the first scientific observation of the Miage glacier, the debris-covered tongue whose lateral moraine walls the right-hand side of these flats. It is the third largest glacier in Italy, and it carries so much rock on its surface that below about 2,500 m the ice is hidden completely. Saussure is the same naturalist who noticed the out-of-place sandstones up at the Col du Bonhomme on our second day.

eras.label: Forbes maps a lake nobody had drawn
eras.text: The earliest record of the ice-contact lake held against the Miage moraine is the 1:25,000 map made by James David Forbes, the Scottish physicist whose Alps work argued that glaciers flow like a viscous fluid. His map shows a small lake on the west side of the present basin with ice filling the rest. Martino Baretti's survey of 1880 found three basins totalling 22,000 square metres; the Courmayeur cadastral map of 1893 shows the lake cut to 10,000 after the glacier pushed 110 m into it. Federico Sacco surveyed it again in 1917 and 1918.

eras.label: The big lake drains away
eras.text: The Lac de Combal proper was a far larger body of water, dammed across the Val Veny by the Miage glacier and its right-lateral moraine. It survived into the early twentieth century and then went, leaving the marshy plain we walk across, drained by the meltwater of the Allée Blanche and Estellette glaciers. The braided flats and the shallow pools are the sediment trap the lake left behind, filled in.

eras.label: Still being measured, now for the risk
eras.text: The observation has not stopped, but the reason for it has changed. A slow drainage of the Miage lake in September 2004 was documented in detail; a far more violent outburst on 26 August 2014 sent enough water down the valley to damage the river embankments below. After nearly a century of little change, the lake grew quickly between 2015 and 2019, and it is now monitored by drone and satellite survey to estimate how much water could come out at once.

entries.summary: Built in 1982 by an alpine guide as a memorial to his climbing partner, who was killed in an aircraft five years earlier at thirty-five. The two of them had made the first Italian ascent of the Nose of El Capitan together, and the refuge exists because one of them outlived the other. Reaching it means walking the balcony path out of Courmayeur: it is about nine kilometres off route if we take the Val Ferret bus to Arnouvaz instead, so on that version of the day we never come near it.

eras.label: Giorgio Bertone, who came for the mountains and stayed
eras.text: Bertone was born at Borgosesia in Piedmont in 1942, drawn first to Monte Rosa and then to the valleys under Mont Blanc. He moved to Courmayeur in his early twenties and made himself, against real financial difficulty, first a ski instructor and then an alpine guide. In the early 1960s, with the Tuscan climber Cosimo Zappelli, he opened hard direct lines on the Brenva face and the Aiguille Croux; their 1964 route on the north-east spur of the Pointe de l'Androsace is still seldom repeated. He was also a mountain rescuer. A Courmayeur guide who knew him put it plainly: there was no alternative, either he climbed it or the mountain came down.

eras.label: Killed on a training flight
eras.text: In August 1977 Bertone died in an aircraft crash below the summit of Mont Blanc du Tacul, on a training flight with a student pilot. He was thirty-five. He had by then climbed and in many cases first climbed the hardest lines in the massif, and the writer Gian Piero Motti, who thought highly of him, tried in print to understand what had drawn a climber of that calibre to flying.

eras.label: A refuge instead of a memorial stone
eras.text: Lorenzino Cosson — Renzino — was Bertone's rope partner and friend. They had climbed together in Yosemite, taking the first Italian ascent of the Nose of El Capitan, and shared mountain rescue work and photography besides. Five years after Bertone's death Cosson built this refuge at 2,000 m on the Mont de la Saxe and put his friend's name on it. The refuge's own telling of the story keeps an exchange between them from a hard day on a face, when Cosson said: see what sort of climber you have ended up with for a partner. Bertone put out his hand and answered that you can find as many climbers as you like, but not friends — come on, let's go.

entries.summary: Three friends from Courmayeur built this in the 1990s and asked Walter Bonatti if they could use his name. He said yes and came to the opening on 1 August 1998 — the first refuge in Italy to carry it. The terrace looks straight at the Grandes Jorasses, where he made both his first great climb at nineteen and a winter first ascent fourteen years later. Like the Bertone it stands on the high balcony path, a little over three kilometres above the valley road, so it is off route on the day we take the bus to Arnouvaz and only the full walking day goes past the door.

eras.label: Nineteen, on the face you can see from here
eras.text: Bonatti was born in Bergamo in 1930 and arrived on the climbing scene at nineteen, with the sixth ascent of the Walker Spur on the north face of the Grandes Jorasses — the wall directly opposite this refuge — alongside Mario Bianchi, Emilio Villa and Andrea Oggioni. Two years later, with Luciano Ghigo, he made the first ascent of the east face of the Grand Capucin, then the outstanding problem of the massif. He came back to the same Jorasses face in January 1963 for its first winter ascent.

eras.label: K2, and the answer he climbed alone
eras.text: At twenty-four Bonatti was the youngest man on the Italian K2 expedition. He carried oxygen to 8,100 m with the Hunza porter Amir Mahdi and the two were forced to bivouac in the open at that height, which nobody believed survivable. He said for the rest of his life that the summit pair had left them; the expedition denied it for decades and he was not vindicated for roughly fifty years. His answer was on rock: in August 1955 he soloed a new route up the south-west pillar of the Petit Dru, six days on the face with five hanging bivouacs, retrieving his own pitons so that every metre gained cost him three. It is still called the Bonatti Pillar.

eras.label: Frêney, then a deliberate ending
eras.text: In the summer of 1961 he was on the Central Pillar of Frêney, on the Italian side of Mont Blanc within sight of this valley, when a storm caught seven climbers near the top. Bonatti organised the retreat and four of them died, Oggioni among them. He kept climbing — the north face of the Grand Pilier d'Angle in 1962, the Walker Spur in winter in 1963 — and then chose his ending. Between 18 and 22 February 1965, in the centenary year of the Matterhorn's first ascent, he soloed a new direct line up its north face in winter. He announced his retirement from serious climbing immediately afterwards, at thirty-five, and spent the rest of his working life as a reporter for Epoca. He died in Rome in 2011.

eras.label: A refuge named with his permission
eras.text: The refuge came out of a friendship between Pierre Sicouri, an industrialist who climbed these mountains, Sergio Favre, an alpine guide and architect who roped up with him, and Flavio Guichardaz, a local surveyor and builder who knew the ground. Bonatti was often a guest of Sicouri's at Villa MacKenzie down in the Val Ferret, so the name was not borrowed from a stranger. Building started in July 1996, the shell and roof were up in 1997, and it opened on 1 August 1998 with Bonatti there. For the first years a room in it was set aside as la maison de Walter, where he stayed when he came.

entries.summary: A refuge built of local stone and larch just after the First World War, flattened by an avalanche in 1960, and left as an empty site for three decades before being rebuilt in 1992 on its own foundations.

eras.label: Stone and larch at the head of the valley
eras.text: The first refuge here went up shortly after the First World War, built from local stone and larch timber at the Pré de Bard alpage under the last climb to the Grand Col Ferret. Its position — the final shelter on the Italian side before the Swiss border — made it an immediate fixture for the early walkers and climbers coming through the Val Ferret.

eras.label: Destroyed by an avalanche
eras.text: An avalanche took the building away completely, ending several decades of use in a single winter. The site was not rebuilt. For the next three decades there was nothing here but foundations, at a point on the route where a shelter is genuinely useful, and walkers crossing the col had to do without it.

eras.label: Rebuilt, and still being handed on
eras.text: The refuge was rebuilt from its own foundations in 1992, deliberately continuing rather than replacing what had been lost. A further renovation in 2020 added sustainable systems while keeping the older fabric. In 2025 the Chanoine family — Elena and Armando and their five children, several of them guides or ski instructors — bought the Pré de Bard mountain and the refuge from the Decarolis and Donnet family, who had owned and built it.

entries.caveat: This account comes almost entirely from the refuge's own history page, which is the only detailed source available and is not independent. Its arithmetic is also loose: it says the site lay empty for thirty-five years but dates the destruction to 1960 and the rebuilding to 1992, which is thirty-two. And it does not say who Elena was.

entries.summary: The trail runs straight down the main street of the last village in the Swiss Val Ferret that was lived in all year round. Its stone houses and larch granaries are unusual enough that an art historian living in the valley spent years cataloguing them before they were sold off, and the village is also the setting of a novella from 1865 about a boy the commune hired out.

eras.label: A valley owned by the Hospice
eras.text: Thomas, Count of Savoy, gave the forests of Le Clou and Ferret, at the head of this valley, to the Hospice of the Grand-Saint-Bernard. For close to seven centuries the Hospice held the right to take timber out of them — on the order of a hundred cubic metres a year, to heat a building at 2,469 m that could not grow its own fuel — and the men of the valley earned a little money cutting and hauling it. The wood went out over the Pas des Chevaux at 2,680 m, a pass named for the horses and mules that carried it. The arrangement was argued over for centuries and ended in 1893, when the bourgeoisie of Orsières bought the right out for 15,000 francs. In 1910 the railway reached Orsières and brought coal with it, and the question stopped mattering.

eras.label: The goatherd of Praz-de-Fort
eras.text: Eugène Rambert — professor of French literature at Lausanne and then at the polytechnic in Zurich, and one of the founding members of the Swiss Alpine Club in 1863 — set a novella in this village. Gaspard Gros is an orphan, and the commune places him out at ten as cheap labour to a hard man down at Le Châble in the Val de Bagnes, where the work and the beatings leave him hunchbacked. At thirteen he is sent back here and given the village goats, more than sixty of them, to herd alone. When the job passes to a younger placed child he goes to Rossinière in Vaud, falls in love with a girl who is promised elsewhere, walks back into the Valais mountains and kills himself. It appeared fifteen years before Heidi and reads as its exact opposite: the same figure of a boy alone on a mountain with animals, and none of the consolation.

eras.label: Glacier ice, and where it went
eras.text: Before refrigeration, keeping food was constant work, and a valley with glaciers in it had an advantage. Blocks were cut from the Saleinaz glacier above the village and sent down chutes built out of tree trunks to Praz-de-Fort, loaded onto carts under tarpaulins for the road to Orsières, and put on the railway. They went to towns across Switzerland and, by the valley's own account, as far as Paris. The trade ran until 1914.

eras.label: A survey of what was left
eras.text: Frédéric Künzi, an art historian living in the valley, watched these buildings go: some collapsing, some converted to garages, some taken apart and rebuilt as luxury chalets in Verbier. He set out to record what the commune of Orsières had actually built, published the result in 1998 and laid out a waymarked trail through Praz-de-Fort, Les Arlaches and Issert so anyone could read the buildings off the ground. What he was recording: houses of stone rather than the timber usual elsewhere in Valais, walls 60 to 120 cm thick under slate roofs quarried locally, windows kept small and almost none facing north. Barns and granaries in slow-grown larch, the trunks split down the middle so the dense heartwood faces the weather, which is what gives old façades their mahogany colour. And the raccard, the building for threshing and storing rye, which stands clear of the ground on grès — squat piers each capped with a thick round disc of slate, so a dormouse climbing the pier meets an overhang and drops off. Its threshing floor is laid in heavy planks, grooved and tongued, so the flail loses no grain between the boards. Many are jointly owned, which you can read off double doors split by a post cut with boundary crosses. The older ones carry rosettes, sun-wheels and the monogram IHS, with the owner's initials, the letters FF for fieri fecit — had it made — and the date, always on the lintel over the main door.

entries.caveat: The name is explained locally as pré des fours, the meadow of the kilns, for the lime kilns that burnt the local limestone into the mortar holding these walls up. Praz is certainly the Latin pratum, a meadow, but no toponymic authority establishes the second half and the kiln reading is village tradition rather than scholarship. Two of the sources here also contradict themselves. The trail booklet says in one sentence that the valley's cart road was built in the middle of the nineteenth century, and in the next that a hay cart could not get up the valley at that date, which cannot both be true — a twentieth-century date is far likelier. And the heritage panel heads its account of the ice trade “around 1920” while saying in the text that the glacier was worked until 1914.

entries.summary: A few paces below the road on the way into Champex there is a door in the rock that was an official secret until 1999. Behind it is artillery fort A 46: six hundred metres of gallery cut into the south ridge of the Catogne, ten guns firing from four casemates, and quarters for a garrison meant to be sealed in and go on working. It was the hinge of the whole fortified system guarding the road to the Great St Bernard, and you can go inside it.

eras.label: Falling back into the mountains
eras.text: After France collapsed in June 1940 and Switzerland found itself ringed by the Axis, the Swiss army gave up the idea of holding the plain and withdrew into the Réduit national, fortifying the mountains instead. Valais mattered for what crosses it, and over a little more than a century some 380 bunkers, artillery works and tank barriers were built in the canton. Work on A 46 ran from 1940 to 1943, driven entirely into the rock at the foot of the Catogne's south ridge, 500 m above the basin of Orsières. Its job was to close the only two ways through — the road over the Great St Bernard and the road into the Val Ferret — and to give fire support to the infantry holding that axis against an attack out of Italy.

eras.label: Ten guns and a town underground
eras.text: The armament was eight 10.5 cm guns and two of 7.5 cm, firing from four casemates and covered by six anti-aircraft guns. Below and around it, infantry works at Château Roc, Manoday and Le Biolley carried fortress machine guns and 8.1 cm mortars to stop anyone reaching the casemates on foot. Inside, the galleries held magazines, a telephone exchange, an officers' mess, a kitchen, dormitories, machine rooms with filters and generators, and a water tank fed from a spring, so the place could be shut and live on itself. Champex also housed the fire-control post for the sector, coordinating the guns of Champex, Commeire, Follatères and Dailly, which is what made it the pivot rather than simply the largest.

eras.label: Kept for a war that did not come
eras.text: Through the Cold War the fort was modernised and rebuilt against the possibility of nuclear attack, and stayed in service long after the threat it was dug for had gone. The last fortress regiments in Valais were disbanded at the end of 1994, the army used A 46 until 1998, and it was declassified in 1999.

eras.label: Bought by the people who wanted to keep it
eras.text: The association Pro Forteresse was started in September 1992 by ten founding members to save the works along the Great St Bernard axis, and as the army declassified them it bought them — around fifty of the sixty-odd structures in the system by 2002, from high-altitude rock strongpoints to the three big artillery works. The federal inventory of military monuments notes, a little pointedly, that this approach remains unique in Switzerland: the association argues that a single work only makes sense inside the chain it belonged to. Champex opened to visitors in 1999, and the same federal inventory holds it up as the example of what the canton might do with the rest.

entries.caveat: The numbers vary by source and nobody reconciles them. Construction is given as 1940–1943 by the fortification literature and as October 1941 to December 1942 by the regional tourist board. The fort's owners say it could shelter three hundred men, while a widely copied listing puts the garrison at a hundred and fifty; those are probably capacity and establishment rather than a contradiction, but no source says so. Altitude is quoted as 1,450 m in the military sources and 1,473 m elsewhere, against 1,461 m for the visitor entrance in the Swiss federal terrain model.

entries.summary: The lake is natural — meltwater held behind the moraine of a glacier that came down the Arpette valley and left more than ten thousand years ago — but nearly everything around it was built to sell the view of it. Champex went from a summer pasture where two herdsmen put walkers up on straw to nine hotels and five hundred beds in sixty years.

eras.label: A lake, and the bog beside it
eras.text: The basin was gouged and then dammed by the moraine the Arpette glacier left as it withdrew. Sediment cores taken from the bed record the last 14,500 years of vegetation around it, which is why a small resort lake turns up in the scientific literature at all. One of the two inlets on the west side is not natural: it is a bisse, a cut channel bringing water over from the Arpette valley, probably medieval, and from the time it was dug the lake also served as a reservoir for irrigating the meadows down at Orsières. The marshy ground it feeds on the western shore is on the federal inventories of raised bogs and of fens of national importance, and the canton protected 10.3 hectares of it in 1997. It is the only place in Valais where the small cranberry grows and the only one with a bog pine wood.

eras.label: Two herdsmen and a bed of straw
eras.text: Champex was a mayen, one of the middle pastures where the herds stopped on the way up to the alp, and it had buildings for that and nothing else. When the first walkers in serious boots began arriving around 1850, two of the men summering their animals here — Daniel Crettex and François Biselx — took them in, sharing rye bread, cheese and wine from Fully, and giving them a bed of straw in the barn.

eras.label: Nine hotels and five hundred beds
eras.text: The Société anonyme de l'Hôtel-Pension du Lac was formed in 1886 and, after years of building, opened in 1890 with a salon and fireplace, hot meals, finely painted porcelain basins and ewers, and central heating with a boiler behind it, so a guest could have a hot bath. The hoteliers then competed by improving the resort rather than undercutting each other — central heating, the first tennis court, a landing stage on the lake, orchestras they hired between them — and by the time they were finished there were nine hotels and more than five hundred beds. Each called its guests to fixed mealtimes with a bell or a Far Eastern gong, for roast mutton and cutlets. Afternoon tea was the fashion, taken first at Champex d'en Haut, then at the Signal, then at the Alpina, which put on tea dances. The evening of 1 August was the event of the season: fireworks, the lake lit up, a gala dinner, a ball, and a champagne fountain running into the small hours. Getting here was a two-hour carriage ride up from Orsières, or three and a half from Martigny.

eras.label: Roads, and a heated pool because the lake is cold
eras.text: The cantonal government opened the Valettes road in 1926 and the commune of Orsières built the road up from Orsières in 1929, which is when motor coaches could finally reach the resort. The hoteliers had got ahead of that in 1911, when their syndicate asked the commune to require a public enquiry for every building application — a deliberate piece of restraint that is part of why the place still hangs together visually. Down at the water they added changing cabins, public lavatories and a free beach, none of which changed the fact that the lake sits between 14 and 17 degrees; in 1960 a company was formed to build a heated swimming pool instead. The Breya chairlift followed in 1952, built after Verbier opened its pistes, and Champex spent forty years attached to Verbier's lift company before going its own way again.

entries.caveat: The belle-époque account comes almost entirely from the regional tourist board's own history page, which cites nothing. Its load-bearing dates — the 1886 company, the 1890 opening, the two roads in 1926 and 1929 — are repeated consistently elsewhere, but the detail that makes the story worth telling, the gong and the champagne fountain and the names of the two herdsmen, rests on that single page. It does not date the nine hotels and five hundred beds at all; that count is given in passing, alongside the 1911 building rules.

entries.summary: A rock garden of some four thousand mountain plants, laid out from 1927 around a Swiss industrialist's holiday chalet and opened to the public four years later. It is a side trip from the village rather than a stop on the trail — a few minutes on foot from the lake, uphill, with an entrance fee and closing time. In September 2025 the foundation that runs it took its founder's name off the institution, having commissioned the research into his life and then published what it found.

eras.label: A cable manufacturer buys a parcel at Champex
eras.text: Jean-Marcel Aubert (1875–1968) was born at Le Brassus in the Vallée de Joux and founded a cable and wire works at Cossonay in 1898, which he built into an international business over twenty-four years and was dismissed from at the end of 1922 after a quarrel over wartime production. The historian who went through that company's archives describes him as quick, enterprising and clever, and also as greedy, unscrupulous and willing to manipulate his partners to get what he wanted. In 1925 he bought a 600 m² parcel of ground at Champex, and a garden began to grow around the holiday chalet he kept there.

eras.label: Correvon lays out the alpinum
eras.text: Aubert commissioned Henry Correvon (1854–1939), the Geneva horticulturist who was the authority on alpine rock gardens and had built one at Bourg-Saint-Pierre in 1889, to make an alpinum around the chalet. It opened to the public in 1931. In 1953 Aubert brought in Egidio Anchisi, a pupil of Correvon's, to give the garden a landscape form, and the shape it has now is largely his. It holds about four thousand species, twelve hundred of them from the Alps and Valais, and is listed on the federal inventory of cultural property of national importance; Patrimoine suisse gave it the Schulthess garden prize in 2007, for a garden made in the era when tourism first threatened the alpine flora and now used to study it.

eras.label: What he did in France
eras.text: Aubert had moved to France in 1923 and sold and repaired American cars — Ford and General Motors — through several companies. From July 1940, under German occupation, his business multiplied roughly tenfold and was done almost entirely with the occupying authorities: maintaining and repairing their vehicle fleet, trading vehicle parts on their account, manufacturing war materiel including tank-transporter trailers, tank tracks, seaplanes and Krupp tractors, a stake in a firm pouring concrete for the Atlantic Wall, huts for occupation troops, and a purchasing office that bought them whatever they asked for. He also took an active part in aryanisation — the removal of Jews from economic life — buying the furniture business Le Bucheron and, together with a French textile industrialist, the Galeries Lafayette, part of whose capital he passed on to German financial interests. The historians put the turnover at about 1.2 billion French francs and the profit above 100 million, of which 52 million was his. He was arrested on 31 August 1944, moved to hospital under police guard and escaped in February 1945, was rearrested that May and escaped again eight days later, and got back to his chalet here. The stolen shareholdings were returned to their owners in the autumn of 1944. Between 1947 and 1950 a French court sentenced him in his absence to national degradation, life imprisonment, confiscation of his property and a ban from French soil. The historians' verdict is that he was not a Nazi but a businessman who treated an occupation as an opportunity, and went on doing so to the end.

eras.label: The foundation looks, and changes its name
eras.text: Aubert signed the founding act on 22 May 1967 and endowed the foundation with 500,000 francs, handing the running of the garden to the botanical gardens of the city of Geneva and the botany institute of the university of Neuchâtel; both withdrew in 2007, and the canton of Valais and the commune of Orsières have run it since. Preparing for the garden's centenary in 2027, the foundation commissioned a life of its founder in 2023, and the first report came back in March 2024 with the Galeries Lafayette in it. Rather than let it rest there, it appointed an independent committee — an ethicist from Geneva, a historian who had worked on the Bergier commission into Switzerland's wartime conduct, and a historian from Paris 8 — and published their findings in full. They concluded that the money that made the garden, all of it spent before the war, came from clean Swiss industry, and that the 1967 endowment could not be traced to the occupation profits, so nothing was owed to anyone. They also recommended that the foundation stop carrying his name. On 25 September 2025 it did, becoming simply the Fondation du Jardin botanique Flore-Alpe.

entries.caveat: The foundation is the source both for the case against its founder and for the finding that it owes no restitution, which is an institution marking its own paper — though publishing the historians' report in full is the opposite of burying it, and the two historians are independent of it. They are explicit about the gaps: a Swiss company registered at Champex, the Société Nouvelle de Capitalisation, was financially active during the war and the French archives say nothing about it, and Aubert's frequent wartime crossings between France and Switzerland cannot be explained from any surviving record. The garden's founding dates vary by source: the foundation's own chronology has a 600 m² parcel bought in 1925 and the alpinum begun in 1927, other accounts give 500 m² in 1924, and the regional tourist board has him arriving in 1923 and buying a chalet called La Sapinière that year. The same tourist page has him dying in 1967, the year he signed the foundation over, rather than 1968. The chronology used here is the foundation's.
